text.p: Digital Equipment Corp late Tuesday called a move by Intel to have a judge decide part of its breach-of-contract case without a trial "a purely diversionary tactic."

"Intel's filing of a partial summary judgement motion is another attempt to divert attention from the real issue between the parties - Intel's infringement of Digital's patent," said Digital spokesman Dan Kaferle.
"We will answer the motion in due course, although it is hard to understand why it was filed...Our view again is that the motion is a purely diversionary tactic," he said.

The world's largest chip maker earlier Tuesday asked the U.S. District Court in San Jose, Calif. to rule that it does not have to supply Digital with Pentium computer chips past the third quarter, when a supply contract between the companies expires.

Intel, based in Santa Clara, Calif., is suing Digital to force the computer maker to return confidential documents about Intel products in the works. PC makers such as Digital rely heavily on these documents to plan their own product offerings.
Intel asked for these documents back shortly after May 13, when Digital sued Intel in the U.S. District Court in Worcester, Mass. for allegedly infringing on some of its patents on chip technology.

Digital sells many more Intel chips than its own 64-bit high speed Alpha chips. Kaferle said the Maynard, Mass. computer giant "has strictly observed confidentiality terms under which these documents (about Intel's long-delayed 64-bit chip) were provided."

In the motion, Intel said it had a right to ask for its documents back under a contract between the companies. Because "there can be no dispute about the material fact," Intel wants the judge to rule on the case without a jury, the motion said.
Digital officials said they are examining Intel's motion, and had no further comment.
Intel also said in the motion that it does not have an obligation to supply Digital with Pentium chips beyond the third quarter when the purchase order runs out.
"Intel is no more obligated to continue to provide DEC with Intel confidential information than it is obligated to continue to provide DEC with Intel processors," Intel said.

But Kaferle replied, "We regard Intel's statements concerning supply...as nothing more than an attempt to create uncertainty in the marketplace. We are attemptting to maintain normal commercial dealings with Intel while our lawsuit is pending.
"If any (supply) issues do arise, we are confident we will be able to make arrangments to ensure an adequate supply of chips to our customers," Kaferle said..
Digital executives have said they have a "long-standing" supply agreement with Intel, which would prevent Intel from cutting off the supply.
